sections.title: Enrolling a child in swimming lessons
sections.context: You will hear a father phoning an aquatic centre in Brisbane to enrol his daughter in swimming lessons.

transcript.speaker: Bridget
transcript.text: Good morning, Westside Aquatic Centre, Bridget speaking.

transcript.speaker: Sanjay
transcript.text: Hi there. I'd like to enrol my daughter in swimming lessons for next term, please. Are there still places?

transcript.speaker: Bridget
transcript.text: Yes, there should be. Let me open the enrolment form. Could I start with your surname?

transcript.speaker: Sanjay
transcript.text: It's Donnelly.

transcript.speaker: Bridget
transcript.text: Is that D-O-N-E-L-L-Y?

transcript.speaker: Sanjay
transcript.text: Almost. There are two Ns. It's D-O-N-N-E-L-L-Y.

transcript.speaker: Bridget
transcript.text: Is this her first time at our centre?

transcript.speaker: Sanjay
transcript.text: Yes. We've only just moved to Brisbane from Wellington, and she learned a little at a school pool there, but she's been away from the water for about a year.

transcript.speaker: Bridget
transcript.text: That's quite common, and children usually pick it up again very quickly.

transcript.speaker: Bridget
transcript.text: Thank you. And how old is your daughter?

transcript.speaker: Sanjay
transcript.text: She's seven. Well, she'll be eight in February, but she's seven at the moment.

transcript.speaker: Bridget
transcript.text: That's fine. We group the children by their age at the start of term, so I'll put 7. Can she swim at all?

transcript.speaker: Sanjay
transcript.text: A little. She's happy putting her face in the water, and she can swim a few metres with a kickboard, but she can't do freestyle without it.

transcript.speaker: Bridget
transcript.text: Then she'd go in Level 2. Level 1 is for children who are just learning to float, and Level 3 is for children who can swim a full length by themselves. So Level 2 sounds just right.

transcript.speaker: Sanjay
transcript.text: Great. Which days are the classes?

transcript.speaker: Bridget
transcript.text: Level 2 runs on Tuesdays and Thursdays. Tuesday afternoon is very popular and it's already full, I'm afraid. I have a few places on Thursday.

transcript.speaker: Sanjay
transcript.text: Thursday's fine. She finishes school at three, so we could easily get here by four.

transcript.speaker: Bridget
transcript.text: There are two Thursday classes. One starts at four o'clock, but that's for Level 3. The Level 2 class is at 4:15, and it lasts forty minutes.

transcript.speaker: Sanjay
transcript.text: So 4:15. That's ideal.

transcript.speaker: Bridget
transcript.text: Wonderful. Now, the fee. A term is ten weeks, and the cost is 216 dollars.

transcript.speaker: Sanjay
transcript.text: Right. Is there any discount?

transcript.speaker: Bridget
transcript.text: There is. If you pay for the whole term before it starts, instead of paying week by week, we take 24 dollars off. So you'd pay 192 dollars.

transcript.speaker: Sanjay
transcript.text: That's a good saving. I'll pay it all upfront.

transcript.speaker: Bridget
transcript.text: Lovely. The new term begins on Monday 26 January, but that's a public holiday for some of our classes. Yours is a Thursday, so the first lesson will be on 29 January.

transcript.speaker: Sanjay
transcript.text: Sorry, the twenty-ninth?

transcript.speaker: Bridget
transcript.text: That's right, 29 January. Please arrive about ten minutes early so she can get changed.

transcript.speaker: Sanjay
transcript.text: Okay. Is there anything I need to tell you about her health?

transcript.speaker: Bridget
transcript.text: Yes, we ask every family. Does she have any medical conditions we should know about?

transcript.speaker: Sanjay
transcript.text: She has mild asthma. She carries an inhaler, and I'll make sure she brings it every week.

transcript.speaker: Bridget
transcript.text: Thank you, that's really helpful. I'll make a note so the instructor knows, and she can keep the inhaler beside the pool. Is she allergic to anything?

transcript.speaker: Sanjay
transcript.text: No, just the asthma.

transcript.speaker: Bridget
transcript.text: Good. Now, I need your home address, for our records.

transcript.speaker: Sanjay
transcript.text: It's 47 Lomandra Street, in Toowong.

transcript.speaker: Bridget
transcript.text: Sorry, was that 74?

transcript.speaker: Sanjay
transcript.text: No, 47. Four, seven.

transcript.speaker: Bridget
transcript.text: Thanks. And the postcode?

transcript.speaker: Bridget
transcript.text: Perfect. I'll email you the confirmation and a receipt as soon as the payment goes through. Do you have a few more minutes? I'd like to tell you about the changing rooms and parents' area.

transcript.speaker: Sanjay
transcript.text: Sure, I'd like to know.

transcript.speaker: Bridget
transcript.text: Well, there's a family change room just inside the entrance, which has lockers that take a two-dollar coin. Parents can watch the lessons from the viewing area upstairs, which has a window onto the pool. There's also a small café there, and it serves coffee and snacks.

transcript.speaker: Sanjay
transcript.text: That sounds lovely. And what should she bring?

transcript.speaker: Bridget
transcript.text: A swimsuit, a towel, goggles if she likes them, and a swimming cap if she has long hair. It's also a good idea to bring a drink bottle, because the pool is warm and the children get thirsty.

transcript.speaker: Bridget
transcript.text: Also, if she misses a lesson because of illness, she can attend a make-up class in the same term, as long as you call us before four o'clock on the day.

transcript.speaker: Sanjay
transcript.text: That's very good to know.

transcript.speaker: Sanjay
transcript.text: Thank you. I think that's everything.

transcript.speaker: Bridget
transcript.text: You're welcome, Mr Donnelly. We'll see you on the twenty-ninth.

sections.title: The Harbour to Park Fun Run
sections.context: You will hear the race director giving a final briefing for a charity fun run in Auckland.

transcript.speaker: Keira
transcript.text: Good morning, everyone, and welcome to the final briefing for the Harbour to Park Fun Run. My name's Keira, and I'm the race director. First of all, thank you for choosing to run for such a good cause. Every dollar you've raised goes to the children's hospital, and last year we raised over a hundred thousand dollars between us.

transcript.speaker: Keira
transcript.text: Let me go through the course, section by section, so you know what to expect on Sunday. The race is eight kilometres. We start at Waterfront Park, and you'll see the big inflatable arch from a long way off. On the ground there's a timing mat, and I'd ask you to run across it, because that's how your time is recorded. If you're walking with a pram, please start at the back.

transcript.speaker: Keira
transcript.text: From the park, the route follows Pohutukawa Drive, along the water's edge. This is the flattest section, and the best part for settling into a rhythm. There's a local band playing at the roadside, and last year, many runners said they sped up when they heard the drums.

transcript.speaker: Keira
transcript.text: At about the three kilometre mark, you turn up Bluff Road, and I should be honest with you. This is a steep hill, nearly half a kilometre long. Don't try to run up it as quickly as the flat. Slow down, take smaller steps, and keep your head up. Remember, it's the hardest part of the course, and once you're at the top, it's mostly downhill.

transcript.speaker: Keira
transcript.text: After the hill, you reach Sandy Bay, where the road runs along the beach. The water station is here, in the middle of the beach car park. Please take a cup, drink it, and put it in the bin. We don't want to leave rubbish on the beach. There'll be a second station near the finish.

transcript.speaker: Keira
transcript.text: At six kilometres you cross the old Mill Bridge. The bridge is only two metres wide, so it's very narrow, and it's difficult to overtake. If you're running faster than the people around you, please wait until you're over the bridge before you try to pass. Everyone's finish time is recorded by the timing mat, so a few seconds won't matter.

transcript.speaker: Keira
transcript.text: The last stretch takes you into Memorial Lawn, where the finish line is. The photographer will be standing near the line, and the photos will be on our website by Monday, free of charge, so remember to smile. Unfortunately, the ice-cream van that was there last year can't come this time, but there will be fruit and sports drinks for everyone.

transcript.speaker: Keira
transcript.text: Now, some practical information. First, where do you leave your things? If you've brought a bag, you can leave it at the bag drop beside the start. It's free, but please put your name on a label, and don't leave anything valuable in it, because we can't be responsible for phones or wallets. We'd suggest you keep your keys in a pocket.

transcript.speaker: Keira
transcript.text: Next, the fundraising. Many of you have been collecting money online, and thank you. If you're still collecting sponsors, you can continue until Friday after the race. Anyone who raises more than 200 dollars receives a free T-shirt, which you can collect at the finish.

transcript.speaker: Keira
transcript.text: And please don't forget to warm up. The race begins at nine o'clock sharp, and we'll lead a short warm-up at the start line at a quarter to nine, with music. It's a lot of fun, even for people who don't think of themselves as athletes.

transcript.speaker: Keira
transcript.text: A word about the medals. This year, for the first time, they're made from recycled materials. They were designed by students at the local art school, and every finisher receives one, whether you run, jog or walk. We'd like to thank the school for that.

transcript.speaker: Keira
transcript.text: The final point is about volunteers. We're still short of about twenty marshals for the course, especially at the bridge, and at Sandy Bay. If you have a friend or family member who isn't running and who'd like to help, please ask them to sign up at the table by the door. Volunteers get a free breakfast and a cap, and they're a very important part of the day.

transcript.speaker: Keira
transcript.text: Finally, the weather. At the moment the forecast looks good, but it can change quickly at this time of year, so please check the website on Saturday evening. If there's a thunderstorm, we may delay the start, but we'll let you know by text message. Thank you for listening, and good luck on Sunday.

sections.title: A rainwater harvesting project
sections.context: You will hear two engineering students, Mei and Oscar, discussing a report with their tutor, Doctor Barrett.

transcript.speaker: Doctor Barrett
transcript.text: Hello, Mei, hello, Oscar. Come in. I've read your draft report on the rainwater system for the community garden. Overall, it's a good start. Let's go through it.

transcript.speaker: Mei
transcript.text: Thanks, Doctor Barrett. We'd like to check that the design is realistic before we finish the report.

transcript.speaker: Doctor Barrett
transcript.text: Remind me why you chose the garden at the primary school.

transcript.speaker: Oscar
transcript.text: Mainly because Perth gets so little rain in summer, and the garden uses a huge amount of drinking water. We thought that if the roof of the hall could supply the garden, we'd save the school quite a lot.

transcript.speaker: Mei
transcript.text: And the teachers were really keen. They've even offered to let us test the system once it's built.

transcript.speaker: Doctor Barrett
transcript.text: That's valuable. Now, let's start with the gutters. You've drawn the standard plastic ones.

transcript.speaker: Mei
transcript.text: Yes. We've chosen them because they're cheap and easy to fit.

transcript.speaker: Doctor Barrett
transcript.text: That's fine, but make sure you mention maintenance. In Perth, the gum trees drop leaves and bark all year, and the gutters clog quickly. They'll need cleaning at least twice a year, so you should put that in your maintenance schedule.

transcript.speaker: Oscar
transcript.text: Okay, we hadn't thought about the maintenance at all.

transcript.speaker: Mei
transcript.text: Should we also include a cleaning plan for the tank itself?

transcript.speaker: Doctor Barrett
transcript.text: Yes, briefly. Every few years someone has to empty it and check the inside for sludge, and the school should know exactly who is responsible for that.

transcript.speaker: Doctor Barrett
transcript.text: Next, the first-flush diverter. Why is it in your design?

transcript.speaker: Oscar
transcript.text: It sends the first few litres of rain away, because that water washes the dust and bird droppings off the roof.

transcript.speaker: Doctor Barrett
transcript.text: Exactly. And note that in Western Australia it's required by the building regulations for a system that supplies garden taps, so you can't take it out, even if you're short of money. Make that very clear in the report.

transcript.speaker: Mei
transcript.text: Right. Now, the tank. I was hoping to bury it, to save space.

transcript.speaker: Doctor Barrett
transcript.text: I understand, but an underground tank is much more expensive, because of the excavation, and it's harder to inspect. For a school budget, an above-ground tank is the better choice, and it's easier to clean.

transcript.speaker: Mei
transcript.text: Fine. I'll change that.

transcript.speaker: Doctor Barrett
transcript.text: And the pump?

transcript.speaker: Oscar
transcript.text: We've specified a small electric pump. At first, we thought of running it from solar panels, to make the whole system independent.

transcript.speaker: Doctor Barrett
transcript.text: It's a nice idea, but at this scale the panels would cost more than the pump, and the saving is tiny. Stay with the mains. And, by the way, the pump you've chosen is a good deal. I've looked at the prices, and it's cheaper than you estimated in your table.

transcript.speaker: Oscar
transcript.text: Oh, good. Then we might have some money left for other things.

transcript.speaker: Doctor Barrett
transcript.text: Lastly, the overflow pipe. When the tank is full, the extra water goes through the pipe, and you've shown it open at the end.

transcript.speaker: Mei
transcript.text: Yes, so it drains into the garden bed.

transcript.speaker: Doctor Barrett
transcript.text: That's fine, but mosquitoes love tanks, so the end of that pipe must be covered with fine mesh. Otherwise they'll breed in the water, and the school will have a problem.

transcript.speaker: Oscar
transcript.text: Understood. I'll add that to the diagram.

transcript.speaker: Doctor Barrett
transcript.text: Now, let's talk about the report itself. I like the structure, but it's missing a few things. Tell me what you plan to change.

transcript.speaker: Mei
transcript.text: Well, the introduction is too long, isn't it? It's nearly two pages.

transcript.speaker: Oscar
transcript.text: I wouldn't cut it. The background on Perth's climate is important. I think the problem is in the later sections. We need a diagram of the layout, because it's hard to follow without one.

transcript.speaker: Doctor Barrett
transcript.text: I agree with Oscar. A clear diagram showing the roof, the gutters, the diverter and the tank would help a lot. And you also need a table of costs, so the reader can see the price of each part and the total at a glance.

transcript.speaker: Mei
transcript.text: All right. We'll add both. I think the introduction can stay as it is, and the conclusion is fine too.

transcript.speaker: Doctor Barrett
transcript.text: It is, but do add a sentence about future work. Now, what will you do next?

transcript.speaker: Oscar
transcript.text: We have to decide how to test it. I was going to suggest we measure the amount of water collected after each storm.

transcript.speaker: Mei
transcript.text: But there might be no storms before the deadline. I'd rather build a small model and test it with a hose.

transcript.speaker: Doctor Barrett
transcript.text: That's a good compromise. If it rains, record the real results as well, but don't depend on it. And please book the workshop now, because it fills up quickly.

transcript.speaker: Oscar
transcript.text: We'll book it today.

transcript.speaker: Mei
transcript.text: One more question. How many references do you expect in the final report?

transcript.speaker: Doctor Barrett
transcript.text: At least ten, and preferably more from recent Australian sources. The council guidelines on rainwater use were updated last year, so check you have the latest version rather than the old one.

transcript.speaker: Oscar
transcript.text: I found a government website with a calculator for roof catchment. Could we use that for our estimates?

transcript.speaker: Doctor Barrett
transcript.text: Yes, but explain your assumptions, such as the roof area and the average rainfall per month. A number with no explanation is worth very little.

transcript.speaker: Mei
transcript.text: We'll set that out in an appendix.

transcript.speaker: Doctor Barrett
transcript.text: Good. And think about the school's needs, too. A system that works on paper but that the teachers can't maintain is not much use, so keep the instructions short, with plenty of photographs.

transcript.speaker: Oscar
transcript.text: Maybe a one-page guide for the caretaker.

transcript.speaker: Doctor Barrett
transcript.text: A very good idea.

transcript.speaker: Doctor Barrett
transcript.text: Excellent. Send me the revised report in two weeks.

sections.title: Glaciers in the Southern Alps
sections.context: You will hear a geography lecturer talking about glaciers in New Zealand and how they are changing.

transcript.speaker: Doctor Hale
transcript.text: Good morning, everyone. Today I'd like to talk about glaciers in the Southern Alps of New Zealand, and what is happening to them. New Zealand is a good place to study this, because its glaciers are unusual. They flow down from high mountains to quite low altitudes, so they respond quickly to changes in the climate.

transcript.speaker: Doctor Hale
transcript.text: Let me begin with the biggest one. The longest glacier in the country is the Tasman, which is about twenty-three kilometres long and runs down the eastern side of Aoraki Mount Cook. Visitors often take boat trips on the lake at its end. But that lake is itself a sign of change. Since the early nineteen nineties, the end of the Tasman Glacier has retreated by more than 5 kilometres, and the meltwater has collected in front of it, forming a lake that is growing every year.

transcript.speaker: Doctor Hale
transcript.text: Why does this matter for glaciers? Well, a lake at the front accelerates the process. The water is warmer than the air, and it melts the ice from below. In addition, pieces of ice break off, which scientists call calving, and float away. So once a lake forms, the glacier can lose ice much faster than before.

transcript.speaker: Doctor Hale
transcript.text: How do we know all this? Researchers use several methods. The most famous is the annual snowline survey. Each year, at the end of summer, a team flies along the Alps in a small plane and photographs the snowline on about fifty glaciers. The snowline is the boundary between the snow that lasts through summer and the bare ice below. If the snowline moves higher up the mountain, the glacier is losing mass. These photographs go back to nineteen seventy-seven, so they're a very valuable record.

transcript.speaker: Doctor Hale
transcript.text: To work out how thick the ice is, scientists use radar equipment. A radar unit is pulled over the surface, or carried by a helicopter, and it sends signals into the ice, which bounce off the rock beneath. The time they take to return tells us the depth. Some of the glaciers are more than five hundred metres thick, but the ice at the end is thinning rapidly.

transcript.speaker: Doctor Hale
transcript.text: Another tool is satellite imagery, which can show the whole length of a glacier at once, though it is less precise than a person with a measuring tape standing at the edge. Local guides also contribute, because many of them have photographed the same ice for twenty years, and their pictures show changes that no instrument recorded.

transcript.speaker: Doctor Hale
transcript.text: And what is causing the loss? The main factor is temperature. Since 1900, the average temperature in New Zealand has risen by about 1 degree Celsius. That sounds small, but for a glacier it's very significant. A warmer climate affects glaciers in two ways. More ice melts in summer, and in winter, more of the precipitation falls as rain rather than snow, especially at lower altitudes. That means there is less snowfall to replace the ice that has melted. If the snow doesn't build up, the glacier cannot feed itself.

transcript.speaker: Doctor Hale
transcript.text: A useful way to think about a glacier is as a bank account. Snowfall is the income, and melting is the spending. For several decades now, the account has been overdrawn, and the balance gets smaller every year.

transcript.speaker: Doctor Hale
transcript.text: Now, let's look at the consequences. The first is on rivers. At the moment, melting glaciers send extra water downstream, and this has increased the risk of flooding in some valleys, because more water enters the rivers in a short time. Local councils have already built stronger banks in several places. In the long term, however, the opposite will happen. When the glaciers have shrunk, summer flows will fall, and some rivers will become much smaller.

transcript.speaker: Doctor Hale
transcript.text: That matters because many of these rivers are used by people. Farmers on the Canterbury Plains rely on glacier-fed rivers for irrigation, and several hydropower stations also depend on them. If the flow drops in summer, when demand for water is at its highest, there could be serious problems for both farming and electricity.

transcript.speaker: Doctor Hale
transcript.text: There are also effects on tourism. Glacier walks and helicopter flights bring in many millions of dollars each year. At Franz Josef, the track to the end of the glacier has been moved several times, and the glacier is so much shorter that guides now take visitors by helicopter to higher parts of the ice. Some businesses are already adapting, but others fear for the future.

transcript.speaker: Doctor Hale
transcript.text: So what does the future hold? The models vary, depending on how much greenhouse gas we emit. In the most pessimistic scenario, New Zealand's glaciers could lose up to 90 percent of their volume by the end of this century. Even if emissions fall quickly, we are likely to lose about half. In other words, some change is already certain, and the question is how much more we allow.

transcript.speaker: Doctor Hale
transcript.text: For next week, I'd like you to read the two papers on the course page, and consider how the data from the snowline survey could be used to explain this to the public. Thank you.
